n: In this lecture we become acquainted with psychotropic substances, in particular the derivatives of barbituric acid. Within the topic we will consider their physicochemical properties, narcological significance, microcrystalloscopic analysis and colour reactions. During the class, among the barbiturates, we will study barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, hexenal, thiopental and benzonal. Methods of isolation, TLC screening, UV-SP, GC and HPLC will be covered in the next lecture.

First, about barbituric acid itself. Barbituric acid, that is, malonylurea, is not used in medicine. But its derivatives, that is, barbiturates, are widely used in medicine and have great narcological significance. Barbiturates are synthesised mainly from malonic acid and urea. By introducing various radicals, more than 2500 barbiturates have been synthesised. At present more than 50 of them are used in medicine worldwide.

Now the use of barbiturates. In medicine they are used as sedatives, hypnotics, anaesthetics and antiepileptics. At the same time barbiturates show addictive properties, so their narcological significance is great. The dosage forms are varied: tablets, capsules, elixir, injectable solution, powder, suppositories and others. That is, one group of substances can be both a therapeutic agent and a source of addiction risk.

On international control. According to the 1971 UN Convention, 12 barbiturates have been placed under international control. Schedule II contains one substance: secobarbital. Schedule III contains four substances: amobarbital, butalbital, cyclobarbital and pentobarbital. Schedule IV includes allobarbital, barbital, butobarbital, phenobarbital and others, 7 in all. The table shows the same distribution: in Schedule II 1, in Schedule III 4, in Schedule IV 7 substances.

Control in Uzbekistan. On the basis of Resolution No. 330 of the Cabinet of Ministers of the Republic of Uzbekistan of 12 November 2015, 13 types of barbiturate have been listed. Schedule III includes allobarbital, barbital, barbital sodium, butalbital, butobarbital and vinylbital. Also on this list are mephobarbital, pentobarbital, secbutabarbital, thiopental sodium, phenobarbital and cyclobarbital. At present barbital, phenobarbital, hexenal, barbamyl, aethaminal, benzonal and butobarbital are used in medicine, that is, 7 substances.

Properties of the main barbiturates. All the barbiturates listed are white crystalline powders with acidic properties. The degree of acidity is shown by pKa: for phenobarbital 7.4, for barbital 8.0, for amobarbital 7.9, for pentobarbital 8.0. The melting points differ from substance to substance: for barbital 188-192, for phenobarbital 174-178, for amobarbital 156-158, for pentobarbital 129-130 degrees. These figures help to distinguish the substances from one another.

Now let us look at the data sheet of several substances. Allobarbital has a molecular mass of 208.2, pKa 7.8, and melting point 173 °C. It dissolves in water in the ratio 1:700, in ethanol 1:15, in diethyl ether 1:20. Amobarbital has the formula C11H18N2O3, molecular mass 226.3, pKa 7.9, melting point 156-158 °C. Barbital has the formula C8H12N2O3, molecular mass 184.2, pKa 8.0, and melts at 188-192 °C. It dissolves in water 1:130, in hot water 1:13, in ethanol 1:14, in diethyl ether 1:35, in chloroform 1:75.

The next three substances. Butalbital has the formula C11H16N2O3, molecular mass 224.3, pKa 7.9, melting point 188-192 °C. It is sparingly soluble in cold water and soluble in hot water. Butobarbital has the formula C10H16N2O3, molecular mass 212.3, pKa 8.0, melts at 124-127 °C, and is practically insoluble in water. Cyclobarbital has the formula C12H16N2O3, molecular mass 236.3, pKa 7.6, melting point 171-174 °C. It dissolves in water 1:800, in ethanol 1:5.

Three more substances. Pentobarbital has the formula C11H18N2O3, molecular mass 226.3, pKa 8.0, melting point 129-130 °C, and is very sparingly soluble in water. Phenobarbital has the formula C12H12N2O3, molecular mass 232.2, pKa 7.4, and melts at 174-178 °C. It dissolves in water 1:1000, in ethyl alcohol 1:8. Secbutabarbital has the formula C10H16N2O3, molecular mass 212.2, pKa 8.0, melting point 165-168 °C. It dissolves in water 1:1400, in ethyl alcohol 1:12.

Let us compare the solubility of barbital and phenobarbital. Barbital dissolves in water 1:130, in hot water 1:13, in ethanol 1:14, in diethyl ether 1:35, in chloroform 1:75. Phenobarbital dissolves in water 1:1000, in ethyl alcohol 1:8, in diethyl ether 1:13, in chloroform 1:40, in petrol 1:700. The table shows that phenobarbital is much less soluble in water and more soluble in alcohol. Both substances dissolve in alkali solutions.

Solubility of amobarbital, pentobarbital and butobarbital. The molecular mass of amobarbital is 226.3; it dissolves in water 1:1300, in ethanol 1:15, in chloroform 1:17, and does not dissolve in petroleum ether. Pentobarbital is very sparingly soluble in water; it dissolves in ethanol 1:4.5, in chloroform 1:4, in diethyl ether 1:10, and is also soluble in acetone and methanol. The melting point of butobarbital is 124-127 °C; it dissolves in ethanol 1:5, in diethyl ether 1:10, and is practically insoluble in water.

On the sodium salts. Thiopental sodium is a white, sometimes yellowish substance with a faint smell characteristic of sulphur. It is freely soluble in water and ethanol and insoluble in diethyl ether. Melting point 156-159 °C, neutral in nature. The molecular mass of barbital sodium is 206.2, and it is also neutral. It dissolves in water 1:5, in hot water 1:2.5, in ethanol 1:400, and its melting point is 190 °C.

Additional data sheets. Vinylbital has the formula C11H16N2O3, molecular mass 224.3, pKa 8.0, melting point 90-92 °C. It is very sparingly soluble in water and soluble in organic solvents. Secobarbital has the formula C12H18N2O3, molecular mass 238.3, pKa 7.9; very sparingly soluble in water, freely soluble in ethanol and diethyl ether. Barbital sodium has the formula C8H11N2NaO3, molecular mass 206.2, pKa 8.0, is neutral, melting point 190 °C. Vinylbital and secobarbital have acidic properties.

General properties of barbiturates. All barbiturates, except thiopental sodium, are solid crystalline substances, odourless and bitter in taste. They are freely soluble in diethyl ether, less so in chloroform and alcohol, and poorly soluble in water. Another important property: at high temperature they undergo dry distillation. The crystals of the sublimate obtained are characteristic of some barbiturates, so this feature can be used in analysis.

Barbiturates are divided into three groups by duration of action. The long-acting ones include barbital and phenobarbital. The medium-acting ones are barbamyl and aethaminal. The short-acting ones are hexenal and butobarbital. The table shows the same three columns: long, medium and short. This division will be needed later for understanding metabolism and excretion in the urine.

Melting points of barbiturates of narcological significance. For barbital it is 189-191 °C. For phenobarbital 174-177 °C; it dissolves in cold water 1:1100, in boiling water 1:40, in alcohol 1:10. Barbital dissolves in cold water 1:170, in boiling water 1:15, in alcohol 1:14. Barbamyl, that is, 5-isoamyl-5-ethylbarbiturate, is a white amorphous powder, odourless, melting at 141 °C. The melting point of Nembutal is 129.5 °C.

Hexenal, thiopental and benzonal. Hexenal is a white, odourless crystalline powder of rather bitter taste; melting point 143-146 °C. It dissolves in water and alcohol and does not dissolve in ether. The melting point of thiopental is 156-159 °C; it is readily soluble in water, readily soluble in alcohol, and insoluble in ether. Benzonal is a white crystalline powder of bitter taste; sparingly soluble in water, and readily soluble in alcohol, chloroform and ether.

Toxicological significance. Although barbiturates are poisonous, they are used in medicine, and therefore cases of poisoning are frequent. The lethal dose is 20 times the therapeutic dose: for barbital 6-10 g, for phenobarbital 4-6 g. Some barbiturates are cumulative. Pathological-anatomical examination gives no characteristic signs. Therefore the forensic chemical analysis of the biological object and the determination of the amount are extremely important.

Metabolism of barbiturates. In poisoning, part of the barbiturates is broken down in the liver and neutralised, and part is excreted by the kidneys in the urine. Metabolism proceeds in several directions: dealkylation, hydroxylation and carboxylation. The metabolic scheme is given in the book as Figure 20. So, in analysis one must take into account not only the unchanged substance but also its routes of elimination.

t: Excretion of barbiturates in the urine
n: Excretion in the urine. 70-80 per cent of the barbital taken and 15-20 per cent of the phenobarbital are excreted in the urine. Long-acting barbiturates are not broken down much in the liver and are excreted in the urine. Short-acting hexenal and thiopental are rapidly broken down in the liver; they are distributed to the internal organs almost equally. The period of persistence in biological objects is given as from 1.5 to 14 months. In poisoning the urine must be examined.

Signs of poisoning. The poisoned patient sleeps for a long time, sometimes does not wake for 1-2 days, and breathes with snoring. Blood pressure falls, the limbs begin to grow cold, and sometimes nausea and vomiting occur. In the end death results from paralysis of the centres controlling respiration and the blood vessels. That is, the process begins with prolonged sleep and leads to paralysis of the centres.

t: Classification of detection reactions for barbiturates
n: Classification of detection reactions. In detecting barbiturates, colour, precipitation and microcrystalloscopic reactions and physicochemical methods are used. For a pure powder, determination of the melting point, the reaction with alkali and the isonitrosobarbituric acid reaction are carried out. For small amounts, cobalt ammoniate and reactions with cobalt salts in the presence of isopropylamine are used. The choice of reaction depends on the form of the isolate or powder and on the amount of the substance.

t: Melting point and reaction with alkali
n: Melting point and reaction with alkali. The first step is to determine the melting point; the properties of some barbiturates are given in Table 15. Barbiturates are stable to acid and alkali solutions. Only when heated with alkali at high temperature do they break down, and the smell of ammonia is noticed. The smell of ammonia is common to all barbiturates. If acid is added to the product obtained, the smell of the corresponding acid is noticed.

The isonitrosobarbituric acid reaction. If perhydrol and ammonium chloride are added to the residue and heated, an oxidation product is formed. On heating with Na2S, barbituric acid is formed, and with nitrites, red isonitrosobarbituric acid. This acid with iron salts passes into a blue ferrous complex. So the colour changes in sequence: from red to blue.

The reaction with cobalt ammoniate. All barbiturates with an ammoniacal solution of cobalt salts in the presence of methyl alcohol form a characteristic red colour. Filter paper impregnated with cobalt nitrate solution is taken, the alcoholic solution containing the barbiturate is applied to it, and the paper is held in ammonia vapour. As a result a characteristic red colour appears. Remember: purine alkaloids and substances containing a biuret chain interfere with the reaction.

The chemical scheme of the cobalt ammoniate reaction. Co(NO3)2 and 2NH4OH interact to form Co(OH)2 and 2NH4NO3. Co(OH)2 is immediately oxidised to Co(OH)3. With ammonia it gives the complex [Co(NH3)6](OH)3. In place of two hydroxyls in the complex, a barbiturate residue is attached, and a red complex is formed. The colour appears precisely as a result of this attachment.

t: Reaction with cobalt acetate and isopropylamine
n: The reaction with cobalt acetate and isopropylamine. Alcoholic solutions of cobalt acetate and isopropylamine are added to the chloroform solution and shaken. If barbiturates are present, a red-pink colour forms. Here a red inner complex is formed: cobalt is bound with the barbiturate and isopropylamine. Thus the reagents, combining in the alcoholic solution, indicate by colour the presence of a barbiturate.

Microcrystalloscopy. This method is based on identifying substances by crystal structure, size and colour. Under the microscope one examines not the substance itself but the crystals of the products it forms with specific reagents. As for the history, M.V. Lomonosov was the first to use the microscope in chemical research. T.E. Lovitz used the microscope for identification by crystal shape.

Advantages of microcrystalloscopy. First, a very small amount of substance is sufficient for analysis. Second, the method can be used in the analysis of explosive and poisonous substances. Third, filtration, evaporation and heating are not required, so the structure of the substance does not change. That is, the method is simple, safe and does not destroy the sample.

Crystal size and the microscope. Microcrystalloscopic reactions are carried out on a glass slide: first the substance is applied dropwise, then the reagent is added, and the crystals are examined under the microscope. The crystals formed should be 20-50 µm in size. Under the microscope, particles of 2-20 µm can be seen at a magnification of 150-250 times. These indicators serve as the basis for correct evaluation of the crystals.

Crystal and crystal lattice. Solids whose particles are arranged in a definite order, periodically repeated in form, are called crystals. The crystal lattice is the regular periodic arrangement of the atoms and other particles of the crystal; its smallest part is the elementary cell. In ideal crystals the elementary cells are very similar. Real crystals differ from ideal ones, and a mosaic structure is often observed in them.

Conditions of crystallisation. Crystallisation proceeds in two stages. First the centre of crystallisation forms, then the crystal grows through the attachment of ions and molecules. To obtain large crystals the first stage must proceed slowly; for this the reagent is applied to dilute and hot solutions. Conversely, if a concentrated reagent is applied to a concentrated solution, small, uncharacteristic crystals form.

t: Technique of the method: the moist chamber
n: Technique of the method. At the edges of the drop evaporation is strong, so crystallisation begins at the edges of the drop. Placing the substance and the reagent close to each other and joining them with a glass rod gives a good result. If the reaction is slow, the glass slide is placed in a moist chamber: this is a Petri dish and moistened filter paper. After that the process of crystallisation is observed.

t: Crystal shape and drawbacks of the method
n: Crystal shape and drawbacks of the method. The crystal shape depends on the nature of the substance and the conditions: temperature, foreign substances, the solvent and the state of growth have an effect. Sometimes a crystal of a certain shape may fail to form; the causes are concentration, volume, rate, pH, temperature and polymorphism. Many substances give similar crystals, which lowers specificity. Therefore a comparison control must be carried out.

The reaction with concentrated sulphuric acid. The method is based on the fact that barbiturates readily dissolve in concentrated H2SO4 and are precipitated on dilution. The residue is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid. Then on dilution with water a white turbidity forms. The precipitated crystals of most barbiturates have a characteristic shape, by which they can be distinguished.

t: Reaction with copper salts and pyridine
n: The reaction with copper salts and pyridine. If copper-pyridine reagent is added to a residue containing a barbiturate, an amorphous or crystalline precipitate is formed. The compound formed is a complex of the barbiturate with copper(II) and pyridine molecules. Remember: this compound is broken down under the action of mineral acids.

The general scheme of analysis. When working with a powder or residue, determination of the melting point, the ammonia smell with alkali and the isonitrosobarbituric acid reaction are carried out. For small amounts, the reactions with cobalt ammoniate and with cobalt acetate and isopropylamine, as well as microcrystalloscopic reactions, are used. At the next stage TLC screening and UV-SP, GC and HPLC are used; they will be covered in the next lecture.

Conclusion. Barbiturates are derivatives of barbituric acid: more than 2500 have been synthesised, more than 50 are used in medicine, and they have addictive properties. The lethal dose is 20 times the therapeutic dose, and the pathological-anatomical picture is not characteristic, so chemical analysis is decisive. For detection, the red colour with cobalt ammoniate, the isonitrosobarbituric acid reaction and microcrystalloscopic reactions are used.
